title: Hospices and prisons
hookLine: Buddhist chaplains and volunteers in hospices and prisons

lines: A CUSHION THROUGH THE PRISON DOOR.
A CHAIR BY A HOSPICE BED.
cards: A heavy door buzzes. A guard checks a list, then waves through a woman carrying a small round cushion under her arm.
Down the hall, in a plain room with plastic chairs, a handful of men in prison clothes are waiting for her.
Across town, at the same hour, a volunteer pulls a chair close to a hospice bed and doesn't say anything at all for a while. Two very different rooms.
In both, someone from this path has come to sit with people in hard places.

teach.b: Start with a story from the Vinaya. The Buddha and Ananda, walking through the monks' lodgings, find a monk sick with dysentery, lying in his own mess, with no one caring for him.
The other monks say he was no use to them, so they left him. The Buddha sends Ananda for water. The Buddha pours, Ananda washes, and together they lift the man onto a bed.
Then the Buddha gathers the monks and says, in paraphrase: you have no mother and no father here to look after you. If you don't tend one another, who will?

teach.h: WHOEVER WOULD TEND ME, TEND THE SICK.
teach.b: Whoever would tend me, let him tend the sick. Then a story for prisons.
The Majjhima Nikaya tells of Angulimala, a man the text calls a murderer, who meets the Buddha, stops, and becomes a monk. People still fear him.
When he goes begging, stones are thrown and he comes back bleeding, and the Buddha tells him to bear it: the results of what he did are ripening. The story doesn't erase the harm.

It does refuse to say a person is beyond change. Those two stories help explain the modern work. Buddhist chaplains serve in hospitals and hospices, and some volunteers lead meditation groups in prisons.
Some describe their task as presence more than fixing. At a deathbed they may simply sit with someone's breathing, or with a frightened family.
Behind bars, a sitting group may be one of the few quiet rooms in the building. None of it makes hard places easy. It brings a steady person into them.

how: Buddhist chaplains serve in some hospitals, hospices and prisons, and lay volunteers and monastics visit the dying and lead meditation groups behind bars, some describing the work as being present rather than fixing.

games.q: you're one of the monks. a brother monk lies sick and soiled, and he's never been much use to anyone. what does the Buddha do?
o: tells the monks to send him home
sends for water and helps wash him himself
tells him to meditate on his illness alone
games.why: Ananda fetched water, the Buddha poured, Ananda washed, and together they lifted him onto a bed. then: whoever would tend me, let him tend the sick.

practice: Bring to mind someone in a hospital, a care home, a prison, or a long grief; if no one comes, hold all of them, wherever they are.
Breathe in, and picture yourself sitting near them, not talking, just there; breathe out, and wish them steadiness.

wordCard.voice: Gilana. The sick monk the Buddha washed with his own hands, whose care stands behind the chaplains and volunteers who now sit with people in hospices and prisons. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali gilana: sick, ill. the Vinaya's care for the gilana, the sick monk, stands behind today's story.

carryVoice: Your line: in hard places. Presence, more than fixing, is the gift. Day one thousand forty-nine; go gently.
